owned.says: Closing the policy setting dialog with Cancel is reported as a change when Apply was used earlier in that session, and as a cancel otherwise.
The comment box is disabled and reads "Comments unavailable for this policy source" when the source has no comments; otherwise it shows the policy's stored comment, or is empty when there is none.
The Supported on box shows the supported-on name of the policy and is empty when the policy names none.

A policy that applies to both computer and user can be edited for either, starting on Computer when no section was given; a policy for one section is fixed to that section and the section choice is unavailable.
OK and Apply are available only when the chosen policy source can be written to.
The state shown when the dialog opens follows the policy's present state in the source being edited: Enabled, Disabled, or Not Configured for anything else, including an unclear state.
A check box starts with the presentation's default state.
A plain text entry is limited to the maximum length the policy defines and starts with the presentation's default text.
A number entered with a spin box is limited to the minimum and maximum the policy defines, in steps the presentation sets, and starts at the presentation's default.

When the policy is Enabled, each option control is set to the value found in the source: numbers into number boxes, text into text and combo boxes, the matching item in drop-downs, true or false into check boxes, lines into multi-line boxes and the stored list into the list editor.

A drop-down list shows the policy's choices by their translated names, sorted unless the presentation turns sorting off, and preselects the default choice when the presentation names one; otherwise nothing is selected.

A text entry with suggestions is limited to the maximum length the policy defines, starts with the presentation's default text, and lists the presentation's suggestions, sorted unless the presentation turns sorting off.

A plain number box keeps any text a whole-number reading accepts, including a leading sign or spaces; other text is replaced by the default. A number above the maximum or below the minimum is replaced by that limit. Numbers above 2,147,483,647 are replaced by the default even when the policy maximum is higher. Only typing is restricted to digits; pasted text is not. A negative number kept where the minimum is below zero is converted to an unsigned number when applied.
Keys other than digits and control keys are ignored in a numeric text box.
Option controls can be edited only while Enabled is chosen; with Disabled or Not Configured they are greyed out.

Choosing Computer or User in the dialog switches the source, its writability and its comments to that section, and reloads the chosen state (Enabled, Disabled or Not Configured) from it. Option values are replaced only for options the section stores when it is Enabled; other values typed earlier stay in the controls.
When a policy is set to Disabled and the definition gives no off value, its registry value is removed. A defined off value, with any extra off values, is saved instead.
When a policy is set to Enabled and the policy has a registry value name but defines no explicit on value, the value is saved as the number 1.
When a number setting is saved, it is written as text if the definition says to store it as text, otherwise as a 32-bit number.
When a policy is applied and the source supports comments, an empty comment box removes the policy's stored comment and any text replaces or adds it.
OK writes the policy to the source and closes the dialog as a change.

When a list setting is saved, entries that carry their own names are saved under those names. Otherwise each entry is numbered from 1, named with the definition's prefix plus its number, or named after its own text when the definition has no prefix.
A setting that names its own registry key is saved under that key. Otherwise it is saved under the policy's key.
When a multi-line text setting is saved, it is written as a multiple-string value.

When a policy is set to Disabled, each setting gets only its own removal. A list setting has all values under its key removed, even when its definition says to keep other entries. A checkbox with a defined off value or off list gets those saved, and every other setting has its single value removed. Extra values listed for a chosen item, a checkbox's on list and the policy's own on list are left in place.
When Enabled is chosen, applying writes every option of the policy whatever its value, including options never filled in.
When a text setting is saved, it is written as an expandable text string if the definition says so, otherwise as a plain text string.
When a policy is set to Enabled, its own on value is saved and any extra values listed for the on state are saved with it. A key left blank in a list falls back to the policy's key.

When a checkbox setting is saved, a ticked box with no defined on value first saves the number 1, and an unticked box with no defined off value first removes the value. The defined on or off value is then saved, with the extra values listed for that state, and overwrites the first step.
When a list setting is saved and the definition does not say to keep other entries, every existing value under the list's key is removed first. A list with no supplied entries then stays empty.

When a registry value is written for a policy, a value defined as 'delete' is removed, a numeric value is saved as a 32-bit number and a text value as a text string. A policy with no value defined writes nothing.

Applying a policy first forgets everything the source holds for it; Enabled then writes every option's current value, Disabled writes the disabled state, and Not Configured leaves the policy with no values.
When a policy is set to Not configured or Unknown, SetPolicyState writes and removes nothing. Callers forget the policy's old values first, so Not configured works by that removal alone.

When a choice setting is saved, the value of the chosen item is saved together with any extra values that item lists. When the chosen position does not exist, the code fails at that point: values already written for earlier settings of the same policy stay written and nothing undoes them, so the policy is left half set.
When a policy is set to Enabled, only the settings the person supplied are written. A setting with no supplied value is left as it was.
Apply writes the policy to the source, keeps the dialog open and records that a change was made.
When the policy setting dialog is closed by any other means, it is still reported as a change if Apply was used earlier.

reliesOn.says: A name or description written as "$(string.<id>)" shows the language file's text for that id; an unknown id shows the code itself; any other text is shown as written; an empty value stays empty.
For a policy's list elements, a marked-for-deletion list counts as one deleted element, and a list that holds any values counts as a present element and cancels that deletion.
A policy's lists of on-values and off-values count as enabled or disabled evidence for each value in them that is present, using the list's own key when it names one.

A value in a policy file counts as marked for deletion when a deletion marker names it, when the key has a clear-all marker, or when a delete-values list for the key names it, regardless of case. Entries are examined in sorted order, and a value whose name sorts after the marker is stored as present and cancels the deletion, whenever it was written and whichever marker kind came before.
Listing the values of a key in a policy file leaves out the marker entries unless the caller asks for them.
A choice element is read as the position of the first item whose own value is present and, when the item has a value list, whose list is wholly present; when no item matches, the position is -1.
For any other element (number, text, choice, multi-line text), a value marked for deletion counts as a deleted element and a value that is present counts as a present element.
The live registry never reports a value as marked for deletion.

A policy with a registry value of its own counts as enabled evidence when that value holds its 'on' value, which is the number 1 when the template gives none, and as disabled evidence when it holds its 'off' value or is marked for deletion when the template gives none.
Reading a value from a policy file gives nothing when the value is absent or marked for deletion.
A value in the live registry counts as present when its key exists and, unless the value name is empty, the key lists a value of that name, regardless of case. An empty name means the key itself.
If any element is present, the elements add their count to the enabled evidence; only when none is present do deleted elements add to the disabled evidence.
A list element whose entries have names the person provides is read as every stored name with its value, under the element's key.
A list of values counts as present only when every value in it is present.
The saved value of a multi-line text element is read as stored, without first checking that it exists.
A value in a policy file counts as present only if it is stored and not marked for deletion.
A checkbox is on when its on value (or all values of its on list) is present, or, with neither defined, when its value is 1; it is off in every other case, including when its off value is present.

A value counts as present when: for a deletion marker, it is marked for deletion; for a number, it exists as a whole number and equals the expected number; for text, it exists as text and equals the expected text. A value of the wrong kind is not present.
The text of a policy description is tidied for display: leading and trailing spaces are removed from every line and blank space at the end of the text is dropped.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for checking whether a value will be deleted: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.
Text read from a policy file stops at its first empty character, and a multiple-string value ends at its first empty string.

For a checkbox element: a value marked for deletion counts as one deleted element. Otherwise, each present off value (or off-list value) counts a tenth of a deleted element, and each present on value (or on-list value) counts one present element. A checkbox whose template declares no on value or on list adds no present evidence, even if it holds 1.

A source is writable by default for Scratch space; for a registry source it is 'no writing' when the write test failed; for others it is 'no commit' when the file or hive could not be opened for writing.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for reading a value: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.
A stored policy file value is read back as text for text and expandable text, a 32-bit or 64-bit number for numbers, a list of strings for multiple strings, and raw bytes for every other type.

A list element whose entry names do not matter is read as a list of values: when the list has a prefix, the stored values named prefix1, prefix2, and so on, in order, until the first number that is missing; otherwise every stored value name under the key.
The saved value of a number or text element is read as stored; the reading assumes the value exists and is of the right kind, and is not checked first. A checkbox is read by its own rule.

A policy is Enabled when enabled evidence exceeds disabled evidence, Disabled when disabled exceeds enabled, Not configured when there is no evidence either way, and Unclear when both are equal and above zero.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for listing a key's values: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.
Reading a value from the live registry gives nothing when the key is missing. Signed numbers are returned as the unsigned numbers policies use, and environment variables in text are not expanded.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for asking whether a value is present: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.
When a policy file is clearing a key, all values and markers under the key are dropped and a single clear-all marker is stored.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for forgetting a value: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.

When a value is saved into a REG file, it is ignored if a source branch is set and its key lies outside that branch. When no branch is set, every key is accepted. Any value already stored under that name is replaced.

When a value is deleted in a REG file, the request is ignored if a source branch is set and the key lies outside it, or if the key is already marked for removal. When no branch is set, every key is accepted. Otherwise the value is recorded as deleted.
When a policy is forgotten, the whole key of each of its list elements is cleared and every registry value it touches is dropped from the source, so it reads as Not configured.
When a number is saved to the live registry, an unsigned 32-bit or 64-bit number is converted to the signed number the registry stores with the same bits, and the key is created if missing.
In the live registry, 'forgetting' a value deletes it, because the registry cannot remember a pending deletion.
When a value is forgotten in a policy file, both the value and its deletion marker are removed, so the policy reverts to not saying anything about it.
Clearing a key in the live registry deletes every value in it but leaves the key and its subkeys. Forgetting a key's clearance does nothing.
A multiple-string value is stored as its strings each followed by an empty character, with one more empty character closing the list.

When a key's clearance is forgotten in a REG file, the key-removal entry is dropped if it exists. The request is ignored if a source branch is set and the key lies outside it. When no branch is set, every key is accepted.
A 64-bit number is stored in a policy file as 8 bytes, lowest byte first.

The registry values a policy touches are its own value, those in its value lists, those of its elements (the whole key for list elements) and those of checkbox and choice sub-lists, each counted once.
When a key's clearance is forgotten in a policy file, every clear-all marker for that key is removed.

When a key is cleared in a REG file, the request is ignored if a source branch is set and the key lies outside it. When no branch is set, every key is accepted. Otherwise the key's earlier entries are replaced by a key-removal entry.
A 32-bit number is stored in a policy file as 4 bytes, lowest byte first.

When a value is marked for deletion in a policy file, any value or marker already held under that name is dropped first. A deletion marker holding the number 32, as Microsoft does, is added unless the value is already marked or its key is cleared.
When a value is set in a policy file, it replaces any value already held under that name. A deletion marker for the name is not removed.
Text stored in a policy file is written in two-byte characters followed by a closing empty character.
When a value is deleted in the live registry and its key does not exist, nothing happens. A missing value is not an error.
A value written to a policy file is stored as text, expandable text, a 32-bit or 64-bit number or a multiple string by its stated type. Every other type is stored as raw bytes with that type.

owned.says: Open File puts the whole chosen file into the text box, replacing what was typed without asking and without checking it; Reset, after a Yes to "Are you sure you want to reset the text box?", restores the header "Policy Plus Semantic Policy" and blank lines.
Verify reads the SPOL text and reports "Validation successful, N policy settings found." or "SPOL validation failed: " followed by the reason; nothing is applied.
A comment line in a semantic policy script is recognised without regard to letter case. A backslash followed by another backslash is one backslash, and a backslash followed by 'n' is a line break.

A setting value in a semantic policy script is read in this order. Starting with # is a whole number, and a # value that is not a whole number fails with a conversion message. A plain non-negative number is an unsigned number. 'True' or 'False', in any letter case, is a yes/no value. Text in single quotes is text, and text in double quotes is a list of text. 'None' is an empty list. Anything else is refused with 'Unknown option data format.'.
A semantic policy script is refused unless its first line is 'Policy Plus Semantic Policy', with the message 'Incorrect signature.'.
The state in a semantic policy script must be 'Not configured', 'Enabled' or 'Disabled', regardless of case. Anything else is refused with 'Unknown policy state.'.
When a semantic policy script fails to load, the error gives the line it stopped at, in the form '(Error found on line N.)'.
A semantic policy script is read in lines separated by carriage return and line feed. A script using line feeds alone is read as one line, so it is refused with the signature message.

A comment in a semantic policy script is refused when it ends with a lone backslash, with the message 'Escape sequence started at end of comment.'. A backslash followed by any other character is refused with 'Unknown comment escape sequence' naming it.

A policy header line in a semantic policy script is a user policy only when its first word is exactly 'U'. Any other first word, including lowercase 'u' or 'User', is a machine policy. The rest of the line is the policy's identifier. A header with no space after the first word fails with a general index error, with the line number but no reason.

A bracketed setting in a semantic policy script holds one line per entry. Entries with one text are a list, entries with two texts are a table of name and value. With no entries the setting is stored with no value. For a list setting, the existing entries are then removed unless the definition keeps other entries, and nothing is written. For any other kind of setting the empty value makes the write fail.
Settings are read only for a policy that is Enabled. Lines under Not configured or Disabled are not read as settings but as the next policy's header.
Apply accepts only SPOL text that reads correctly; the parsed file is passed back to the main window. Invalid text is refused with "The SPOL text is invalid: " and the reason.
Opening Import SPOL discards any previously parsed SPOL so a cancelled session passes nothing back.
Pressing Escape closes Import SPOL as cancelled unless text in the box is selected; when it is, Escape closes nothing.

actions.name: ButtonCopy_Click
actions.purpose: Selects and copies the whole SPOL text to the clipboard.

actions.name: InspectSpolFragment_Shown
actions.purpose: Focuses the SPOL text and selects it.

actions.name: CheckHeader_CheckedChanged
actions.purpose: Shows or hides the SPOL header line in the text.

actions.name: TextSpol_KeyDown
actions.purpose: Selects all text in the box on Ctrl+A.

reliesOn.says: The fragment text starts with the heading "Policy Plus Semantic Policy" and a blank line only when "Include SPOL header" is ticked; otherwise only the fragment is shown.

actions.name: OkButton_Click
actions.purpose: Collects the grid rows into a list or name-value map, rejecting duplicate names.

owned.says: When the list editor is confirmed for a list where the person names each entry, and two entries have exactly the same name, it is refused with "Multiple entries are named "<name>"! Remove or rename all but one." and nothing is returned. Names are compared exactly, so Run and run are accepted as two entries. A name cell never filled in stops the dialog with an unhandled error.

When the list editor is confirmed for a list without names, every row except the empty new row at the bottom is returned in the order shown, with no check that a cell has content; a row whose value cell was never filled is returned as an empty entry. For named lists the same new row is ignored.

actions.name: ImportSemanticPolicyToolStripMenuItem_Click
actions.purpose: Asks for a semantic policy text and applies it to the policy sources.

owned.says: When a semantic policy is applied, the policy's earlier settings are wiped first and then the stated state and settings are written.

When a semantic policy script is applied to many policies, a policy that fails is skipped and counted, and the rest are still applied. The caller gets only the number of failures, not which policy or why.
A semantic policy script applies each policy to the machine source or the user source by its section.

Importing semantic policy applies all its policies to both sources and comments; the person sees "Semantic Policy successfully applied." or "N out of M could not be applied." when some failed, and the view refreshes either way.

When a semantic policy is applied, a comment is stored for the policy first, only if one is given and a comment store exists, before the old settings are wiped and the new ones written. If the writing fails, the new comment stays against a half-written policy. An empty comment leaves any existing comment alone.

reliesOn.says: A category is orphaned when it has no parent among the loaded definitions although its definition names one.
A category's icon is chosen in this order: orphaned, then empty, then normal.
When a policy is set to Disabled and the definition gives no off value, its registry value is removed. A defined off value, with any extra off values, is saved instead.

A category is visible when empty categories are switched on. Otherwise it is visible only if it has at least one visible policy or one visible subcategory.

A policy is visible only if it applies to a chosen area (user, computer or both). With "Only Filtered Policies" on, it must also pass the filter for a chosen area it applies to; passing for either one is enough.

With both areas shown, a policy that applies to both areas shows its common state followed by "(2)" when both match, the computer state followed by "(C)" when only the user is Not Configured, the user state followed by "(U)" when only the computer is Not Configured, and "Mixed" otherwise.
A filter on state keeps only policies whose state in the checked area is Configured (Enabled or Disabled), Not Configured, Disabled or Enabled, as chosen.
When a policy is set to Enabled and the policy has a registry value name but defines no explicit on value, the value is saved as the number 1.

A multiple-string value is stored as its strings each followed by an empty character, with one more empty character closing the list.

reliesOn.builtBy: an earlier part of this capability

reliesOn.says: When the list is rebuilt, the policy already selected is selected again and revealed only if it is still listed, that is, it sits in the category shown and passes the visibility rule; otherwise nothing is selected. Then, if the policy is in the same category and the list still has that many rows, the earlier top row is put back, so the policy is not guaranteed to stay in view.
A policy passes the filter only when it passes every active part of it.
Text read from a policy file stops at its first empty character, and a multiple-string value ends at its first empty string.
A 32-bit number is stored in a policy file as 4 bytes, lowest byte first.

For a checkbox element: a value marked for deletion counts as one deleted element. Otherwise, each present off value (or off-list value) counts a tenth of a deleted element, and each present on value (or on-list value) counts one present element. A checkbox whose template declares no on value or on list adds no present evidence, even if it holds 1.

When a value is marked for deletion in a policy file, any value or marker already held under that name is dropped first. A deletion marker holding the number 32, as Microsoft does, is added unless the value is already marked or its key is cleared.
When a list setting is saved and the definition does not say to keep other entries, every existing value under the list's key is removed first. A list with no supplied entries then stays empty.
reliesOn.builtBy: an earlier part of this capability

reliesOn.says: For a selected policy the information pane shows its title, "(no requirements information)" when it has no support rule or "Requirements:" plus the support name, and its explanation. A notice that the policy is a preference appears only for preferences.
A policy's icon is chosen in this order: preference, then plain when it has no configurable elements, then "extra configuration" when it has some.
A policy applies to an area when its definition declares that area; a policy declared for both applies to each.
A filter on comments keeps only policies that have a non-empty comment in the checked area, or only those that have none, as chosen.

When a registry value is written for a policy, a value defined as 'delete' is removed, a numeric value is saved as a 32-bit number and a text value as a text string. A policy with no value defined writes nothing.
reliesOn.builtBy: an earlier part of this capability

reliesOn.says: When a policy lists no supported-on information, it counts as supported only if the caller allows unlisted policies. The same applies to a support entry that names no known product.

When a view setting changes, the program moves up to the nearest visible category, drops the selected policy if the move happened or the policy is now hidden, then rebuilds the tree and list. A policy kept after the move appears in the information pane only: rebuilding the list reselects the category in the tree, which clears the selection, so its row is not highlighted.
When a value is set in a policy file, it replaces any value already held under that name. A deletion marker for the name is not removed.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for reading a value: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.
A category is empty when it holds no subcategories and no policies at all, counting hidden ones.

With both areas shown, a policy that applies to one area shows that area's state followed by "(C)" for computer or "(U)" for user. With a single area shown, only that area's state is shown, without a suffix.
When a policy is set to Not configured or Unknown, SetPolicyState writes and removes nothing. Callers forget the policy's old values first, so Not configured works by that removal alone.
reliesOn.builtBy: an earlier part of this capability

reliesOn.says: A stored policy file value is read back as text for text and expandable text, a 32-bit or 64-bit number for numbers, a list of strings for multiple strings, and raw bytes for every other type.
Text stored in a policy file is written in two-byte characters followed by a closing empty character.

When a choice setting is saved, the value of the chosen item is saved together with any extra values that item lists. When the chosen position does not exist, the code fails at that point: values already written for earlier settings of the same policy stay written and nothing undoes them, so the policy is left half set.
reliesOn.builtBy: an earlier part of this capability

reliesOn.says: A policy is Enabled when enabled evidence exceeds disabled evidence, Disabled when disabled exceeds enabled, Not configured when there is no evidence either way, and Unclear when both are equal and above zero.

A policy is a preference, not a managed policy, when it names a registry key outside the three policy locations: software\policies, software\microsoft\windows\currentversion\policies and system\currentcontrolset\policies.
After the category tree is rebuilt from the loaded definitions, no category, policy or highlighted item is selected and the information pane shows the empty state.
When a value is deleted in the live registry and its key does not exist, nothing happens. A missing value is not an error.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for listing a key's values: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.
Reading a value from the live registry gives nothing when the key is missing. Signed numbers are returned as the unsigned numbers policies use, and environment variables in text are not expanded.
When a policy is set to Enabled, only the settings the person supplied are written. A setting with no supplied value is left as it was.
reliesOn.builtBy: an earlier part of this capability

reliesOn.says: A filter on products keeps only policies supported by the chosen products, honouring the options to match any product and to include policies with blank support.
A value written to a policy file is stored as text, expandable text, a 32-bit or 64-bit number or a multiple string by its stated type. Every other type is stored as raw bytes with that type.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for asking whether a value is present: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.

A support entry for a product counts as met in two cases. The entry is not a version range and that exact product is among the chosen products. Or the product has versions beneath it, and any of those versions or their sub-products is chosen, even when the product itself is not.
